A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, title, transport formulation, and original perplexity bound. The complete main texts and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 presents theoretical formulations, proofs in Appendix A, and proposed future work. It reports no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: v3 reports original language-model experiments, computational timings, ablations, and a Monte Carlo simulation in Section 5 and Appendix C. Appendix E supplies generated text samples.

M1.justification: The original minibatch-OT formulation is retained, but v3 adds multimask flows with 50,257 special mask tokens distinct from data tokens and independently adjustable mask embeddings, enabling nontrivial OT couplings for masked-style generation (Section 3.2). It also introduces bound-based masked training variants alongside cross-entropy training (Section 5.2 and Appendix C.2).

E1.justification: v1 evaluates no datasets. v3 adds Morse-converted and character-level Shakespeare experiments, OpenWebText training and text generation, and perplexity evaluation on LAMBADA, WikiText2, WikiText103, PTB, and LM1B. Appendix C.5 additionally evaluates a small synthetic discrete distribution.

E2.justification: v3 introduces comparisons with SEDD and GPT-2 in Table 2, SEDD Absorb in Table 6, and standard-training controls and masked DFM-O/N/S variants in Table 3. DFM-S uses the MD4 loss; MD4 is not a separate additional row. v1 contains no evaluated baseline comparisons.

E3.justification: v3 adds experimental protocols absent from v1: 100k-step Shakespeare training, 400k-step OpenWebText training, batch and sequence-length controls, and comparisons across 8–1024 generation steps. Generation quality is evaluated on 10,240 samples using GPT-2 Large and Llama 3.1 8B, alongside perplexity bounds, entropy, jump counts, and timing measurements.

E4.justification: v3 tests sensitivity to OT regularization, solver choice, and OT batch size; investigates bound tightness through simulation and analytic examples; and checks agreement between dynamic and Kantorovich costs (Section 5 and Appendix C). It also adds diversity and metric-correlation analyses and qualitative generated samples. These investigations are absent from v1.

E5.justification: v3 introduces uncertainty reporting across the empirical evaluation, including plus/minus values for jump counts and standard deviations for generative perplexity, entropy, and ablations (Tables 1, 5, 10–12, 14, and 16). v1 has no such reporting. Repeated-training-run counts, seeds, and the procedure used to estimate these deviations are unspecified.

E6.justification: All empirical results are newly reported in v3. Examples include 85.47 versus 74.87 Morse-code jumps without versus with OT (Table 1), and GPT-2-Large generative perplexity of 141.92 for DFM-MMLM-OT versus 146.54 for DFM-O at 1024 steps (Table 3). Some duplicated BoW scores disagree between Tables 3 and 10; these are internal discrepancies, not changes from v1 results.

T1.justification: The original transport identity and KL upper bound are retained, with the latter becoming Theorem 4.2. v3 adds an exact forward/reverse-velocity KL identity, an entropy identity and second perplexity bound, precise-likelihood expressions, masked-bound equivalence derivations, and a proof of multimask predictive time independence (Theorem 4.1, Propositions 4.3–4.4, and Appendices A.3–A.6).

C1.justification: v3 replaces the speculative chain-of-flows contribution with multimask flows and empirical claims of up to eightfold fewer inference steps for BoW flows at comparable generative perplexity, plus improved multimask generation without reduced diversity. The single evaluation-bound contribution expands to two bounds supporting training and evaluation (abstract, introduction, and conclusion).

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of multimask benefits and expected computational scaling, and qualifies its evaluation claims: OT-coupled bound estimates are heuristic because the implicit coupling is inaccessible, and realistic-scale bound tightness remains unmeasured (Appendices C.3 and C.5). These qualifications go beyond v1's general discussion of source similarity and training stability.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-access statement, three implementation algorithms, and a detailed experimental recipe covering architecture, tokenization, schedules, AdamW settings, warm-up, clipping, hardware, and training time (Appendices B–C). For example, it specifies a 12-layer, 12-head, 768-dimensional transformer and H200 training. v1 lacks these implementation and access details.

R1.justification: v3 adds a dedicated related-work section and substantially expands research positioning. It distinguishes its path-length objective from Shaul et al.'s kinetic-energy approach, acknowledges their concurrent bound derivation, and connects its bounds to Haxholli et al. and Shi et al. It also discusses newer block-diffusion and scaled masked-diffusion work.

P1.justification: Beyond adding scientific content, v3 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and explanatory narrative. It moves Markov-chain background to Appendix D and the original bound derivation to Appendix A.2, relocates training stability into Section 7, removes the chains-of-flows section, and reorganizes the paper around theory, experiments, related work, and structured appendices.

P2.justification: v1 contains no results tables or graphical figures. v3 introduces 17 numbered tables, three formatted algorithms, and seven boxed generated-sample listings. It also changes typography, headers, text width, and appendix navigation, substantially revising how methods and evidence are displayed.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the practical case left untested in v1: controlled language experiments assess generation benefits, computational overhead, bound usefulness, and sensitivity to implementation choices. New proofs and detailed implementation information also improve scrutiny and reproducibility. Inconsistent duplicated BoW scores, unexplained standard-deviation estimation, and heuristic OT-bound evaluation limit precision, but do not outweigh the substantial gain in evidence and technical completeness.
